title: The plan: schema, grill and approval
bridge: A Nova plan is like a PR description written before the code, validated by a zod schema like a form. Except: the definition of done and the QA checks come first, and the requester must press Approve before any code is written.
intro: This lesson defines the plan every Nova run writes before coding. It also covers the questions Nova asks first on bigger tickets, and the Approve / Change / Stop buttons. The plan is what the requester approves and what everything after it is judged by.

sections.h: Start from a plan on a branch
p: After a Nova run plans a ticket, the branch nova/RH-1234 holds one file: .nova/plan.json. Open it and the first key is definition_of_done, in the requester's words. Then qa_plan: 3 to 5 checks, each saying what a user sees. Then the steps, the VM size, an estimate and a risk.

Three programs read this file: the harness in the VM, the orchestrator, and the Slack app that renders it. So its shape lives in the shared package as a zod schema. The field names are snake_case because that is the file format.
A schema is a description of a shape that can check data at runtime. zod gives us both the check and the TypeScript type from one definition.

sections.h: The schema, part 1: a QA check and a step
p: A QA check says in plain words what a user does and sees. It also says what a test reads to confirm it. That is a test ID, an ARIA role, visible text, a row count or an API response. Never a class name. That is the FE review rule, and it is enforced by the enum.
A step names what to do, the files it touches, and the model and effort to use. The defaults are Opus 5.5 at medium, per the routing table.
sections.because: We make the checks concrete and observable up front, so later a tester can run them without reading Nova's code.

notes.text: Check ids are QA-1 to QA-9. The regex rejects anything else, so links from checks.json and the PR table stay simple.
The plain-words line a reviewer and the QA agent read. It describes the screen, not the code.
What the test reads. At least one, and only observable things: no class names, no snapshot dumps.
The level the test is written at. browser_only means the QA agent checks it by hand in a browser.
edge_case defaults to false. The Plan schema later demands at least one true.
The proof the PR will show: a video, screenshots at 760 and 1440, a transcript or test output.
The model per step, defaulting to Opus 5.5. A cheap step can name Haiku.
The five screen states a UI change must say how to reach: loading, empty, error, filled, bad data.

sections.h: The schema, part 2: the plan and its rule
p: The Plan object puts definition_of_done first and limits it to 5 lines. The QA plan has 3 to 5 checks. screen_states is a partial record: a map from some of the five states to a line saying how to reach each one.

superRefine adds a rule that spans fields: the QA plan needs an edge case, and a UI change needs screen states. zod reports it as an issue with our message, and the harness sends that message back to the planner.
sections.because: A rule across fields cannot be expressed per field, so superRefine carries the two rules reviewers care about most.

notes.text: Done comes first, 1 to 5 lines, in the requester's own words. It is what the requester approves.
3 to 5 checks. Fewer is not a plan; more is a test suite, not a plan.
z.partialRecord: keys from ScreenState, each optional. Only UI changes fill it.
The VM size for the build. Planning happens on lite; the plan says what the build needs.
Nova's own estimate in minutes. It drives G3's check-ins and is measured; it is never a limit.
superRefine runs after the field checks and can look at the whole plan.
A plan is a UI change when any step touches frontend/src/.
One custom issue with a clear message. The planner reads it and fixes the plan.
The Plan type for the whole codebase, derived from the schema.

sections.h: The planner step: ask for the shape, then check it
p: The planner is an agent session on a lite VM. It loads the plan-and-grill skill and the codebase skill, reads code, and ends with structured output. z.toJSONSchema turns the zod schema into the JSON Schema the SDK's outputFormat needs.

The option io: "input" matters. It builds the schema for what goes in: fields with a default, like edge_case, are optional for the model. Without it, zod describes the output shape, where every default is already filled in.
The harness still runs Plan.safeParse on the result. The model's JSON matches the schema, but superRefine rules are not in JSON Schema. So safeParse is what catches a missing edge case.
sections.because: The model can only promise the JSON shape; our cross-field rules are checked by code and sent back as a fix request.

notes.text: The JSON Schema for the planner's structured output, in input mode so defaults stay optional.
safeParse never throws. It returns success with data, or an error with a list of issues.
A good plan becomes the typed Plan the rest of the harness uses.
Each issue has a path (qa_plan.2.id) and a message. Joined, they are the fix request the planner gets.

sections.ifInstead: If z.toJSONSchema throws about an unrepresentable type, check that zod is version 4; version 3 has no toJSONSchema.

sections.h: The grill, part 1: hand back or ask
p: For bigger or fuzzy tickets, and whenever readiness says ask, Nova asks before planning. We call this the grill: specific questions, at most 5, each with Nova's default guess. No VM runs while Nova waits.

This block is workflow code inside ticketToPr, right after readiness. It must stay deterministic: no Node APIs, no fetch, no clock. Every model call and every Jira or Slack post is an activity. Its timeout is a safety net, never a work limit.
sections.because: Asking before planning is cheap and avoids plans built on guesses, and a clear small fix skips it entirely.

notes.text: proxyActivities gives typed stubs for activities. Calling one records a command in the workflow history.
waitForPerson is G3-38's helper: a reminder after 1 day, parking after 2, and the Stop button.
LONG = 7-day startToCloseTimeout and 2-minute heartbeats. The 7 days catch a dead worker, nothing else.
checkReadiness from lesson g4-1: one Sonnet call, 5 minutes is plenty.
writeGrillQuestions is an Opus session. It gets LONG so it is never cut off mid-thought.
hand_back means the ticket cannot be done as written. Nova tells the requester why and the run ends.
undefined tells the caller the run is over. No VM was claimed.

sections.h: The grill, part 2: the question loop
p: The loop runs when readiness says ask, or once for any ticket that is not small. Readiness may already hold questions. If not, an Opus session writes them from the ticket text and the skill's "how to ask" section.

Answers come back as the answerQuestion signal, from a Jira comment (lesson g4-1) or the Slack thread. The workflow clears run.answer before posting, so a fast reply is not lost. After the answers, readiness runs again.
A question that keeps coming back is flagged to the requester, not looped on. Two rounds is the limit, and then a person decides how to make the ticket clear.
sections.because: We want one round of good questions, not an agent that keeps asking until the person gives up.

notes.text: Enter when readiness says ask, or on the first round for a bigger or fuzzy ticket.
Use readiness's questions if it wrote any; otherwise ask Opus 5.5 at medium to write them. Still no VM.
Nova state becomes Needs info (lesson g4-1), one of the three states that ping a person.
Clear the answer slot before posting. The signal handler fills it; a reply that lands early is kept.
waitForPerson returns false when the run was parked or stopped. Then the grill ends without a plan.
A short summary of the answers goes onto the ticket, so the ticket stays the source of truth.
Readiness again, now with the answers in the ticket text.
Round two still unclear: flag it and stop asking. A person edits the ticket or replies.

sections.h: The plan message: Approve, Change, Stop
p: The plan is posted as a Jira comment and a Slack message. The Slack version uses Block Kit, Slack's JSON layout language. It has a header, text sections, a context line and an actions block with buttons.

Everything fits one screen: done, the QA checks with the co-sign note, files, estimate, risk, and a link to the full plan. The estimate line says "not a limit" on purpose, so people read it the same way we do.
sections.because: The requester decides from one screen, so the message shows done and the checks and links the rest.

notes.text: The fallback text for notifications and screen readers.
Done first, in the requester's words. This is the sentence they approve.
The QA checks, numbered, with the proof in brackets and the edge case marked.
One context line: files, estimate (not a limit), risk, VM size, model, and a link to the full plan.
block_id plan_decision groups the three buttons. The Slack app handles their action ids.
The value carries the ticket and the plan version. An old button cannot approve a newer plan.
Stop asks for confirmation and says what is kept: the branch and the notes.

sections.h: Who may decide, and what happens next
p: Only the requester's decision counts. The Slack app looks up the clicker's Slack ID in config/people.yaml. Anyone else gets an ephemeral message: "only <requester> can decide this plan". In Jira, "@Nova approve", "@Nova change <text>" and "@Nova stop" do the same.
Change opens a modal for free text. The planner gets the text and posts plan v2. The button value carries the version, so an old Approve cannot approve a plan it never saw.

On Approve, the decidePlan signal arrives. The workflow claims a full VM at once (G3: claim early) and the state moves to Working. While waiting, the state is Awaiting approval. Stop keeps the branch and notes and destroys the VM.

Approving a plan is not approving the PR. The PR still needs exactly one approval from a person who is not the requester. The plan approval is about what to build; the PR approval is about what was built.

callout.text: No code is written before a person approves the plan. The requester approves done and the QA plan together, so the checks Nova is judged by are agreed up front.

quiz.q: Why does the plan start with definition_of_done and the QA checks?

options.text: Because the schema needs a first field
options.why: Order in JSON is not the point. The point is what the requester approves.

options.text: So the requester approves done and the checks together, and Nova is judged by what was agreed
options.why: Writing done and the checks first is why Nova can prove its work instead of claiming it.

options.text: So the planner can skip reading the code
options.why: The planner still reads code on a lite VM; the order is about agreement, not effort.

options.text: A limit: the run stops when it passes
options.why: Nothing cuts a run in the middle. Limits never cut work in progress.

options.text: Nova's own guess, measured and used for check-ins, never a limit
options.why: G3's check-ins ask how it is going past the estimate; the number is learned from, not enforced.
That is a 7-day safety net on the activity, unrelated to the plan.

quiz.q: A teammate who is not the requester clicks Approve in Slack. What happens?

options.text: The plan is approved; any engineer can approve
options.why: Only the requester's decision counts. people.yaml maps the Slack ID to check this.

options.text: They get an ephemeral message that only the requester can decide, and nothing changes
options.why: The Slack app refuses the click and tells them why; the workflow keeps waiting.

options.text: The run stops because the wrong person touched it
options.why: A wrong click is not a stop. Stop is its own button, for the requester, with a confirmation.

words.plain: A description of a data shape that code can check at runtime; zod gives a type from it too.
A zod rule that looks at the whole object and adds an issue with your own message.
The standard JSON way to describe a shape; the SDK's outputFormat needs it.
Nova's round of specific questions to the requester before planning a bigger ticket.
1 to 5 lines, in the requester's words, that say when the ticket is finished.
Slack's JSON layout language for messages with sections and buttons.
A Slack reply only one person sees, used to refuse a click politely.
